## Definition

**Variance** measures the average squared deviation of data points from the mean. It quantifies how spread out the values in a dataset are.

## Formula

**Sample variance:**

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n-1}$$

**Population variance:**

$$\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(X_i - \mu)^2}{N}$$

Note: Sample formula uses n-1 (Bessel's correction) for unbiased estimation.

## Calculation Steps

1. Calculate the mean of the data
2. Subtract the mean from each value (deviations)
3. Square each deviation
4. Sum the squared deviations
5. Divide by n-1 (for sample) or N (for population)

## Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Always positive | Squared values can't be negative |
| Units squared | If data in ms, variance in ms² |
| Sensitive to outliers | Squaring amplifies extreme values |
| Foundation for SD | Standard deviation = √variance |

## Why Square the Deviations?

- Raw deviations sum to zero (cancel out)
- Squaring makes all values positive
- Gives more weight to larger deviations
- Has useful mathematical properties

## Interpretation

| Variance | Interpretation |
|----------|----------------|
| Small | Values cluster near the mean |
| Large | Values spread widely from mean |
| Zero | All values identical |

## R Code Example

```r
# Sample variance
var(scores)

# With missing values
var(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Population variance (divide by n, not n-1)
mean((scores - mean(scores))^2)

# Relationship to SD
var(scores) == sd(scores)^2
```

## Variance vs. Standard Deviation

| Variance | Standard Deviation |
|----------|-------------------|
| Squared units | Original units |
| Harder to interpret | Easier to interpret |
| Mathematically convenient | More intuitive |
| Used in calculations | Used in reporting |

## DataLab Connection

Variance helps compare the consistency of performance across participants. High variance in reaction times at the **Reflex Test** station indicates large individual differences.
